p: Yury Danilovich was the eldest son of Daniel of Moscow, the first prince of Moscow. His first military action was the defence of Pereslavl-Zalessky against Andrey of Gorodets, grand prince of Vladimir. Because Daniel had never held the grand princely title, his descendants had no legitimate claim to Vladimir under the traditional rules of succession. When Andrey died on 27 July 1304, Tokhta, khan of the Golden Horde, therefore gave the title to Yury's uncle, Mikhail of Tver. Yury rebelled, and two campaigns by Mikhail against Moscow, in 1305 and 1308, forced him to accept the khan's decision.

Yury meanwhile arranged the murder of Prince Konstantin of Ryazan, whom his father had captured in 1302 and held in Moscow, and annexed the Ryazan fortress of Kolomna. He also took Mozhaisk, which had belonged to the princes of Smolensk. By 1314 he had the backing of Metropolitan Peter and a military alliance with Novgorod against Tver.

In 1315 he went to the Horde, where he spent two years. His bride Konchaka converted to Orthodox Christianity and was baptised Agafiia. Returning with a large force of Tatars, he approached Tver, but his army was defeated and his wife and his brother Boris were captured; he fled to Novgorod and sued for peace. When his wife died unexpectedly as a hostage in Tver, he told the khan that Mikhail had ordered her poisoned. Both princes were summoned to Sarai, and after a trial Mikhail was executed on 22 November 1318.

As grand prince from 1318 to 1322 Yury was resisted by other princes and by the people, who thought his appointment illegitimate. He was charged with gathering the tribute for the Horde, and in his last two years in the office the khan sent no fewer than four punitive expeditions to the northeastern principalities to enforce it.

In 1322 Dmitry of Tver persuaded the khan at Sarai that Yury had kept a large part of the tribute, and received the patent for Vladimir himself. Yury then led the army of Novgorod against the Swedes, founded a fort at the mouth of the Neva River, signed the Treaty of Orekhovo in 1323 and conquered Velikiy Ustyug the same year. Summoned to the Horde for trial, he was killed by Dmitry on 21 November 1325 before any formal investigation. Dmitry was executed at the Horde eight months later. Early in 1326 Yury's remains were brought to Moscow and buried by the bishops under Metropolitan Peter.

notes: The article calls Mikhail of Tver Yury's 'uncle'; kept as the article has it.
The article has Yury go to the Horde in 1315 and stay two years; the existing entry dates the patent to 1317, which agrees. The article gives no year for the defeat near Tver.
The article spells the khan Uzbeg/Uzbek; the entry has Uzbek Khan, so I avoided the name ('the khan').
The article's lede calls him 'Yury III' once; not used.
